LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Little — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: you will whisper in a little voice, then boom in a big voice and compare, and your child will meet “little” in a real sentence, “A little mouse.” By the end, “little” should be a word they know at a glance.

What is this?

“Little” is a describing word. On this card, a very small boy stands alone surrounded by white space, with the word printed in big, clear letters underneath.

What does it mean?

“Little” describes how a thing looks or how much of it there is, as in “A little mouse.”

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to recognise “little” at a glance, say it clearly, and begin to hear it in the stories you read together. Good hunting grounds: little ducklings, little shoes and little fingers.

Why this matters

Describing words like “little” make a child’s sentences richer and make a book’s pictures easier to talk about.

What it teaches

Describing, comparing and widening vocabulary, plus quick recognition of a high-frequency word.

Words to learn

wordreadpicture

Say this to your child

“Look at this card. It says ‘little’. A little mouse. Now you say ‘little’. Well done!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and read “little” clearly, running your finger under the letters. Let your child say it back, twice.
  2. Look at the picture together: a very small boy stands alone surrounded by white space. Ask what is happening, then link the picture to the word.
  3. Play one tiny game: whisper in a little voice, then boom in a big voice and compare. Read the word one last time and stop while it is still fun.

Look closer at the picture

Point to the word first, then to the picture. Cover the picture with your hand and read the word; lift your hand to check. Then let your child trace the first letter with one finger.

Ask your child

“What does the card say?” “What do you see on the card?” “Can you use “little” in a sentence?” — answered with a read-aloud, a point and a sentence of their own.

What your child can say or do

Expect “little” to appear in your child’s own descriptions all week, sometimes in unexpected places.

Out in the real world

Watch for “little” here: little ducklings, little shoes and little fingers. Every sighting is a free practice round: point, say it, move on.

Try it together

Whisper in a little voice, then boom in a big voice and compare. Finish by saying “little” one more time.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, hold up the card without saying a word. If your child reads “little” straight away, the word has arrived; if not, play the game once more and try again the day after.

Parent tips

Keep it short: five minutes is plenty. Add “little” to the pile only when the cards your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the Little flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).
